title: Natural selection works meaningfully only on simple behavior

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Natural selection works meaningfully only on simple behavior

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The power of natural selection is limited: it can systematically optimize only systems or parts of systems whose behavior is simple, and achieves very little when behavior is complex.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: what I suspect is that in the end natural selection can only operate in a meaningful way on systems or parts of systems whose behavior is in some sense quite simple.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “Fundamental Issues in Biology” (from p. 383), p. 392. Scope: natural selection acting on biological traits

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-14: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.28

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Selection can be measured in restricted experimental landscapes, but the claimed universal boundary between simple and complex behavior is not specified. Current datasets lack representative organismal coverage and comparable complexity measures. Resolving the principle would require extensive new linked genotype, phenotype, and fitness data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across traits with mapped genotype-phenotype-fitness relations, quantify behavioral complexity and the response to selection, then test whether selection response approaches zero above a preregistered complexity threshold. Robust optimization of complex-output traits would refute the asserted limit.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Meaningful operation and behavioral complexity lack standard measures.

Existing fitness landscapes cover a highly biased subset of biological systems.

Selection response is confounded by mutation supply, population size, and environment.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Quantitative genetics can measure whether a chosen trait responds to selection, and that test exists for many simple traits and some complex ones. The claim's partition into quite simple and complex behavior is not a standard variable, so different decompositions give different answers. Existing data constrain examples and do not settle the general limitation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare the response to selection, in breeding data or in evolutionary simulations, for traits graded from simple scalar properties to high-dimensional patterns. Systematic response confined to simple traits would support the claim; reliable optimization of complex patterns would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Artificial selection on complex quantitative traits often works, which pressures the wording but does not map cleanly onto the claim's notion of complexity.

Simple behavior and meaningful optimization are not operational without a chosen trait decomposition.
